identification.summary: Earth Baxia is Trend Micro's name for a suspected China-based threat actor that, per Trend Micro's September 2024 report, targeted a Taiwanese government organization and likely other Asia-Pacific countries using spear-phishing and exploitation of GeoServer CVE-2024-36401 [S1][S2]. Operators deployed customized Cobalt Strike components and a new backdoor Trend Micro named EAGLEDOOR [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro tied the activity to suspicious behavior detected in July 2024 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Name is Trend Micro's Earth-series designation; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources gathered. Trend Micro's own Earth Lusca (a separate cluster) was returned in searches but no source gathered states an Earth Baxia/Earth Lusca relationship; do not merge them.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro assessed the group likely operates from China; coverage describes this as a suspicion, not a confirmed attribution [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Secondary coverage of Trend Micro reports that a Cobalt Strike watermark checked on Shodan linked mostly to machines in China, and that some servers were hosted on Alibaba cloud or located in Hong Kong [S2][S3]. No government attribution or state-sponsor assignment was found.

targeting.notes: Trend Micro named a Taiwanese government organization as the initial victim and said other APAC countries were likely affected [S1]. Security Affairs and The Hacker News report the group primarily targeted government agencies, telecommunications and energy firms in the Philippines, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan and Thailand [S2][S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via spear-phishing emails and exploitation of GeoServer CVE-2024-36401, a remote code execution flaw (CVSS 9.8) that let the actor download or copy malicious components [S1][S2]. Uses GrimResource and AppDomainManager injection to deploy additional payloads [S1]. Deploys customized Cobalt Strike with modified internal signatures and a changed configuration structure for evasion [S1][S2]. EAGLEDOOR is a new backdoor supporting multiple communication protocols for information gathering and payload delivery [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Taiwan government intrusion and APAC activity
campaigns.summary: Suspicious activity at a Taiwanese government organization was detected in July 2024 and tied to spear-phishing and the GeoServer CVE-2024-36401 exploit, with Cobalt Strike and EAGLEDOOR deployed [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Trend Micro publication of Earth Baxia report
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro publicly reported the cluster; trade press described targeting of government, telecommunications and energy organizations in five APAC countries [S1][S2][S3].

diamond.adversary: Suspected China-based actor tracked by Trend Micro as Earth Baxia; no state sponsor named [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing, GeoServer CVE-2024-36401 exploit, GrimResource and AppDomainManager injection, customized Cobalt Strike, EAGLEDOOR backdoor [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Some servers on Alibaba cloud or in Hong Kong per press coverage of Trend Micro's findings [S2][S3]; full IOC list exists in a Trend Micro file not reviewed.
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government organization, and government, telecommunications and energy organizations across the Philippines, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan and Thailand [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing, unpatched GeoServer instances and email users susceptible to spear-phishing [S1][S2].

gaps: WebFetch was blocked in this session; the Trend Micro report, NTT AppDomainManager blog and Trend IOC file were not opened, so details rest on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Exact Trend Micro publication day and secondary-source days are unconfirmed; dates are month-level.
Sponsor, objectives and any government attribution are unknown.
Relationship to other Trend Micro clusters (e.g., Earth Lusca) and other vendor names is unverified.
EAGLEDOOR protocol list (reports mention DNS, HTTP, TCP and Telegram) and the 666666 watermark claim were seen only in unfetched or uncorroborated snippets and are not asserted here.
Spear-phishing lure content, victim counts and post-exploitation objectives are not established.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing geospatial servers (GeoServer) and government email are key terrain in Taiwan and neighboring APAC states [S1][S2]. STEP 2: A critical unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2024-36401) gives the actor a fast path before patching [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish or GeoServer exploit, then Cobalt Strike, then EAGLEDOOR [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued access operations against APAC government, telecom and energy targets; MDCOA is reuse of other public-facing exploits for the same chain. Candidate indicators: unexpected GeoServer child processes, AppDomainManager config abuse, .msc (GrimResource) files in mail, and Trend Micro-published IOCs [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Trend Micro IOCs and GeoServer exposure in partner-nation and supported networks [S1][S2]. Authorities: sharing on allied APAC victims requires coordination through appropriate partner and CTI channels. Mission assurance: patch or isolate GeoServer, harden email against .msc/.NET loader lures, and hunt for modified Cobalt Strike [S1]. Coordination: notify partner-nation CERTs in affected states [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Baxia is a threat actor opearting out of China, targeting government organizations in Taiwan and potentially across the APAC region, using spear-phishing emails and exploiting the GeoServer vulnerability CVE-2024-36401 for remote code execution, deploying customized Cobalt Strike components with altered signatures, leveraging GrimResource and AppDomainManager injection techniques to deliver additional payloads, and utilizing a new backdoor named EAGLEDOOR for multi-protocol communication and payload delivery.
